toc.title: Fawn is not the same as appeasement
What it's like to be in a fawn state

blocks.p: Fawn has officially been added to the growing list of Polyvagal Theory mixed states. Here I'll explain what fawning is and how the Theory interprets it.

The Polyvagal Theory has three brand new additions to the mixed states: appeasement, fawn, and intimacy. Sadly, the new book, Our Polyvagal World, doesn't have much information on this at all. There are maybe two pages, and that's on fawn and appeasement together. They don't talk about fawn in much detail. It's really only a solid couple of lines where they try to explain how it's different from appeasement.

blocks.h: Fawn is not the same as appeasement

blocks.p: As I was researching fawn, I found it's often confused with appeasement, or lumped together with it. Maybe they belong together. I think you could make an argument there, and maybe it's not super important to distinguish the two. But Dr. Porges and his son Seth, who wrote the book, believe they deserve to be distinguished. And I believe Dr. Porges separated the two in a paper on appeasement and Stockholm syndrome as well. So for all intents and purposes, according to the Polyvagal Theory, fawn and appeasement are distinct.

Appeasement involves the activation of all the polyvagal states. I believe they called it a super social engagement, or a super co-regulation, with the evolutionary intent of de-escalating or avoiding a life-threatening situation. For us humans, this would pop up most extremely in a hostage situation or a domestic violence one. The appeaser is joining with their abuser or their captor. They're really aligning their values with their captor's.

Fawning is very similar, I would argue, with the same intention: de-escalation, or reducing the potential of life threat. But instead of a pseudo co-regulation, it's through compliance. It's not the co-regulating of appeasement. As I understand it, fawning is more about invisibility and hiding, existing in a very numb state, I think, and subservience.

Fawning is about surrendering your values and your agency in compliance to the dominant other, the one who is controlling and dominating the situation. It's about quietly attempting to please that other person in order to extend those moments of de-escalation. I think it's very preventative. Fawning involves preemptively anticipating their needs and really not trying to rock the boat, even though that person is already in a situation that is extreme and potentially a life threat. That's very similar to appeasement.
The potential evolutionary intent of fawning is that the predator, or in our case the abductor or abuser, might lose interest.

If the prey, the captive, or the victim of domestic violence can anticipate the needs of the other and preemptively meet them, or keep things calmer by surrendering their own values and empowerment, then the predator might lose interest in them. They might not see them as a threat at all. And that might reduce the defensive activation: the aggressive, bullying, abusive kind of activation.

When I talked with Dr. Porges in my interview with him a couple of episodes ago, he did say that fawning may lead to increased risk. He mentioned murder specifically, and said something about things potentially being more severe.

That makes me wonder whether the predator's state gets amplified in the face of the fawning, worsening the situation. As their state rises and boils over into rage, it has to be targeted toward somebody. Well, it doesn't have to be, but their behavioral adaptation is to target it toward someone they can inflict their dominance on.

So even though the fawner may successfully keep the risk to a minimum for a while, the dominant, abusive captor's stuck state doesn't really go anywhere. Maybe it simmers down enough to get through the day, and the fawner gets their needs met. But I would guess that the dominant person's intense, hidden, frozen, explosive rage is still there. As it boils over, it eventually gets directed toward the person in more of a fawn state, as best I can tell.

That boiled-over rage then reinforces, for the person in a fawn state, that they need to stay in the fawn mixed state. They need to stay compliant. They cannot escape. They must continually be subservient or submissive to the dominant one in the relationship.

The biggest difference between fawning and appeasement might be that, as I understand it, the person who's fawning doesn't need to provide cues of safety. If anything, in these types of relationships, the person fawning probably needs to give no cues of safety, or of flight or fight. They simply need to be hidden, invisible, subservient. They must relinquish all of themselves to the other person so the dominant one doesn't explode in rage.

I imagine that if the fawning person did anything out of line in that relationship, it could trigger the explosive rage in the other person. Any attempt to get out of the situation, to rationalize, to talk to them, to co-regulate, might actually trigger the release of that rage.

In relationships with appeasement, the appeasement seems to work. The appeaser seems able to provide cues of safety without triggering the wrath of the other person. In a fawn relationship, it seems like the role is that shut down, hiding, invisible flavor, plus preemptively meeting the needs of the other. I think that may be what Dr. Porges meant when he said fawning might lead to increased risk.

blocks.h: What it's like to be in a fawn state

blocks.p: Being in a fawn mixed state means a heavy level of enmeshment with the other person's emotions, and being unable to distinguish the self from the other person. A fawn state is going to have a heavy dose of numbness and dissociation. There's going to be a lot of self-sacrifice: trying to fix the other person's problems, blaming themselves, denying their own needs.

I look at it as pleasing versus appeasing. Appeasing is about joining with the other, like a captive who assists their captor in committing crimes or evading authorities, while also providing cues of connection. Pleasing, which is fawning, is more about tending to the needs of the dominant other and overly accommodating what they need, or will need, at the expense of the self.

I kept reading that fawning probably has a lot to do with a history of childhood rejection, shame, neglect, and different types of abuse. It's very much connected to CPTSD, complex post-traumatic stress disorder, and to relational and interpersonal trauma.

There are two paths of trauma. One is the acute life threat reaction, where you go through something, survive it, and are left in a stuck defensive state. The other path is the chronic disruption of connectedness, and that fits more with fawning. That's more connected with CPTSD, in my opinion. It results in a chronic defensive state, which could really be any defensive state.

CPTSD results from the impulse to connect being chronically cut off. Not only cut off, but rejected and shamed as well. So that person's connection impulses never complete. They never get a healthy attachment with a safe other, which is unbelievably important as a foundation in life: being able to identify safety in others, and within ourselves as well. Having a safe other is the foundation we use to build self-regulation, and to offer co-regulation to others in the future.
So what are the states in fawn, now that it's a mixed state? The book pretty much just says it's flight, fight, and shutdown.

I understand the flight and fight state as being used for mobilization. But in this context, the person isn't mobilizing to escape or to be aggressive. They're using that mobilization through hypervigilance, and to meet the needs of the other person.
There's also, obviously I think, a heavy amount of shutdown in fawn. The dissociation, the surrendering, the relinquishing of the self and one's power: that definitely comes from shutdown.

Why would somebody fawn? Why would they stay in an abusive relationship? It's a common question. So let's bring it back to one of our biological imperatives: to find safety. Being in our safety state is what allows us to optimize our resources for health, growth, and restoration. Our bodies are compelled to find homeostasis, to find safety, to self-regulate, and also to receive and give co-regulation.

These fawning relationships don't provide real safety, obviously. But there might be moments of something like safety. In between explosive rage episodes, there may be moments that feel like connection, or a pseudo connection, or close enough to connection. It may feel like protection. It may feel predictable.

It's the same with appeasement. The goal is always safety, to find connection. Appeasement brings a kind of safety. It's not actual safety, but it is some connection, and that might be enough for the body to reach some homeostasis and still use its resources for health, growth, and restoration, at least enough.

With fawning, it's a pseudo safety. Not actual safety, obviously. But there is diminished threat, and there's probably some predictability, and predictability in and of itself is kind of a cue of safety.

That's fawning, and how it could fit into the Polyvagal Theory. I have my questions and my doubts about it. But through this lens, I think fawn connects to flight, fight, and shutdown, and especially shutdown. I think that's a huge part of it. It also connects to the second path of trauma, the chronic disruption of connectedness that leaves somebody in a stuck defensive state. With fawning, I think it's more of a stuck shutdown, with some access to flight and fight.
